title: the seasons
hook: a garden wrung out by summer, then the first rain: the texts split the year into a taking half and a giving half

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: ritu, a season, ritucharya, keeping step with it, and a year that turns six times in the Ashtanga Hridaya.

By the end of a long, hot summer, a garden looks wrung out. The leaves curl. The soil cracks. Even the people tending it move slower, and wilt by afternoon. Then one evening the clouds pile up, the first rain hits the dust, and the whole place smells different. Over the next weeks, green comes back. The classical texts saw the whole year as that kind of rhythm: one half that draws strength out, one half that gives it back.
screen: `A GARDEN WRUNG OUT BY SUMMER.` → `THE FIRST RAIN ON THE DUST.` → `ONE HALF TAKES, ONE HALF GIVES.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita splits the year into two halves, each with three of the six seasons. The first is adana, the taking: late winter, spring and summer, while the sun travels its northern course. Paraphrased, the text says that in this half the sun and the wind grow strong, sharp and dry, and they draw moisture and strength out of the world, and out of people too. The second half is visarga, the giving, or the releasing: the rains, autumn and early winter, while the sun travels south. Here, the text says, the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds, rain and wind, and strength flows back. Not hot season and cold season, but a pulling-away and a pouring-back. The text follows that through to the body. Paraphrased: people tend to be weakest at the turn where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the start of the rains, and strongest at the other turn, in the cold months. That changes how a low stretch looks. If the year itself has a taking half, a tired late summer is partly weather, not character, and the giving half is a time to rebuild, not just recover. The sun's turns matter in Hindu life beyond medicine, too: festivals mark the sun's turn north, among them Makar Sankranti, and some Hindus count the northern course as an auspicious time. The texts take that same turning sky and read it in the body.
screen: `ADANA: THE TAKING HALF` · `VISARGA: THE GIVING HALF` · `WEAKEST WHERE TAKING TURNS TO GIVING` · `A TIRED SEASON ISN'T A FAILING`

segments.voice: As you breathe out, let it be the taking, carrying away what this season has drained: tiredness, tension, the heat of the week. As you breathe in, let it be the giving, the breath coming back slowly, cool and full, with no forcing either one. Then let the breath go on its own; if you pray, you can offer what's been taken and receive what's given.
The seasons. In the Charaka Samhita the year has two halves: adana, the taking, while the sun goes north, and visarga, the giving, while it goes south.
Your line: the seasons. A tired season isn't a failing; the giving half comes round. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners describe the year in two halves, adana and visarga, and adjust diet and activity to protect strength in the taking half and rebuild it in the giving half.
